questions.q: In the lab's $5,000 monthly budget split (15% dev / 25% staging / 60% prod), why is production allocated the largest share while dev gets the smallest?
options: Staging and dev are not real environments and don't need any budget
Development always costs more than production in quantum computing
Production is the revenue/value-generating usage, while most development work runs on free classical simulators rather than billed real hardware
The split is arbitrary and has no connection to actual usage patterns
questions.explain: The allocation reflects that dev work mostly happens on free simulators (per the course's recurring simulator-first development principle), while production work is the actual value-generating, continuously-run workload needing the largest real-hardware budget.

questions.q: With a $750 dev budget and a cost of $30.30 per real-hardware confirmation task on IonQ Aria (1,000 shots/task), how many dev confirmation tasks does this budget allow per month?
options: 30 tasks, rounding $750/$25
750 tasks, treating each dollar as one task
100 tasks, assuming a flat $7.50 per task
questions.explain: $750.00 / $30.30 ~= 24.75, and since you can't run a fractional task, flooring gives 24 affordable confirmation tasks per month.

questions.q: The lab computes a proposed daily VQE re-calibration workload at roughly $101,970/month against a $3,000/month prod budget. By roughly what factor does this exceed the budget?
options: Roughly 3x over budget
Roughly 340x over budget
Roughly 34x over budget
It actually fits within budget with room to spare
questions.explain: $101,970 / $3,000 ~= 34, meaning the proposed workload as originally specified costs about 34 times the allocated production budget -- a mismatch that needs to be caught and addressed before rollout.

questions.q: Why does the lab note that reducing shots from 2,000 to 500 per evaluation cuts COST by 4x but does not cut PRECISION loss proportionally?
options: Reducing shots has no effect on cost, only on precision
Cost and precision both scale identically with shot count, so there's no asymmetry at all
Precision improves when shots are reduced, which is why this lever is attractive
Cost scales linearly with shot count, but standard error (precision) scales as 1/sqrt(shots) -- so a 4x shot reduction increases standard error by only 2x, not 4x
questions.explain: This connects directly to Lesson 17's square-root relationship: cost is proportional to shots, but standard error is proportional to 1/sqrt(shots), so a 4x shot cut only doubles the standard error -- an asymmetry worth exploiting when a workload needs to fit a tighter budget.

questions.q: What does the lab say a good budget justification should include when a proposed workload exceeds its allocated budget?
options: The workload's shape (iterations, shots, frequency), the backend and its pricing, the resulting cost with arithmetic shown, and specific tradeoff options with their cost impacts -- so a non-specialist stakeholder can evaluate the options
A recommendation to silently reduce quality without informing the stakeholder
A request for unlimited budget with no justification needed
Just the final dollar total, with no supporting arithmetic or options
questions.explain: The lab argues that showing the arithmetic and naming concrete tradeoff options (e.g., weekly vs. daily, shot count) lets a non-technical stakeholder actually evaluate and choose among real options, rather than being presented with an unexplained number.
